title: ZTF colour eclipses show that the single-dip old-CPV candidates are M dwarfs with white-dwarf companions, and most old M dwarfs at the x of young CPV hosts are probably such binaries
abstract: Complex periodic variables (CPVs) are young fast-rotating M dwarfs with sharp dips. Tests of whether contraction alone explains their age decline use old main-sequence M dwarfs at the corotation-to-stellar radius ratio x of young hosts. Published TESS tests found 0-4 old CPV labels for 5.3-9.7 predicted, and three old labels have one narrow dip. We folded ZTF g, r and i data (2018-2025) at the TESS ephemerides. All three single-dip candidates (TIC 248394276, 279472930, 446169146) show a stable, flat-bottomed 8-20 min eclipse whose depth falls from 0.29-0.46 in g to 0.03-0.07 in TESS. A blackbody fit gives Teff 5,200-6,700 K and radii of 0.009-0.0135 Rsun at the Gaia distance, i.e. white dwarfs of 0.5-0.9 Msun; dust needs an opacity law steeper than the small-grain limit and fails for two stars. Removing the white-dwarf light puts each M dwarf near the main sequence. A ZTF eclipse search of 1,319 old rapid rotators from four TESS samples finds three more white-dwarf eclipsers (TIC 257216998, 56660560, 165599194). Four of the six are among 26 on-target stars at x < 3.5; corrected for eclipse geometry, about 0.7-0.8 (95%: 0.27-0.99) of those stars are white-dwarf binaries. Young CPVs show no such blue eclipses. Without the eclipsers, at most one old CPV remains, which strengthens the published deficit (p = 0.002-0.024). But if close white-dwarf binaries cannot host CPV material, the corrected denominators give p = 0.05-0.17. Thus no old M dwarf shows young-CPV dips, but most old fast rotators are tidal binaries, and an extra age factor is not demonstrated. Limitations: no spectra, blackbody models, non-blind inspection, 4 eclipsers in 26 stars.
